predictions.text: Forever home purchase seeking others opinions on logistics — We signed a contract to purchase a house with closing in February 2027. The purchase price is $850,000 and we will be putting 5% down so loan will be $807,500. With interest rates climbing, we just want to make sure we aren’t getting into a mess. We can still back out after we have an inspection done. Our household income will be $557,000 starting in December when my wife starts her job. We are both CRNAs so we no concerns with job security or income decreasing. My salary has gone up $100k in the 5 years I have been working as a CRNA. We have a 5 year old and a 1 month old, and possibly will try to have one more child. We have a little over $500k in retirement 401/457. 50k in a HYSA. $75k in a SoFi brokerage account. Currently our monthly spend is around 10k which includes renting a condo at $2,100/mo and $2,000/mo for daycare/nanny. That will increase to $3,000/mo when our newborn starts daycare when she turns 6 months or so. Our first child has $40k in a 529 and I just opened one for our second child and contributing $500/mo. Our gross monthly income will be $46,500. If we both max our 401k and 457, as well as our HSA, our net monthly income will be about $25,000. I’m anticipating our monthly mortgage to be around $7,000, so about 28% of our net monthly income. There should be no reason to be concerned, correct?

First off, bills come first. If you can't pay rent, you have a bigger problem than your investment strategy. Assuming you're talking about after essential bills are paid, if you're paying interest on a credit card... pay it off. Nothing else you can possibly do with your money can beat the return you get by eliminating credit card debt. If you pay 18% interest, then paying down the debt is (more or less) a guaranteed 18% return on your "investment" The only reason to keep cash in the bank is to cover an emergency you can't charge in on the card or for situations where you might lose your access to credit(e.g. you lose your job and they cut your credit line). Once the emergency fund is set up? Pay off the cards.

I have a higher household income than your future state, one child, half the house cost and a third of the current rate and I still feel semi constrained and anxious about our savings rate. An 800k loan at 7% with taxes and insurance folded in is 7k a month, more than your entire budgeted bare minimum expenses. Add to that that homes need care and your bare minimum will go up because of that. Call it 1k a month conservatively. So now 8k + child care, groceries, car stuff, miscellaneous etc. now that 6k looks more like 12k at least. If we assume that you net about 65% of your income and your husbands salary is at the high end of the range, you have a 2500 dollar a month buffer. 65% is the high end, mine after 401k and insurance etc was closer to 55%. Split the difference at 60%. Now monthly income is 13.5k. So if you’re lucky a 1.5k buffer on your bare minimum. Lotta words to say I wouldn’t buy a million dollar house if I were you. Also the whole husband isn’t a saver thing. If you’re married, you have one money. If he’s not a saver, you as a team isn’t a saver. Unless you just mean that he doesn’t think about this stuff and the mental burden falls on you.

I would like to offer that there may not be a bright line difference between “lifestyle inflation” and “sensible family upgrade”. I know people use “lifestyle inflation” negative, but let me offer the alternative view that money is supposed to “inflate” our lives. Its purpose is not to be hoarded like we’re Scrooge, the purpose of money is to be spent. The questions are really, when is the time to spend that money? And are we spending the money in a way that is consistent with our goals? So in practical terms for you and your spouse, I’d say that you both sit down and figure out your plan for your money, including short, medium, and long term goals. See if a newer car can be accommodated in those plans. Then if it’s economically feasible, figure out if it’s what you actually want. At 25 years old, this internet stranger’s opinion is to get something newer if it’s well within budget since one spouse really wants it.

Two HDHP plans for my son - which one is primary/secondary and does it matter? — For 2027, I (dad) will have a HDHP plan. His mom will likely have a HDHP plan as well, but it's possible she'll opt for a non-HDHP plan, so that's still TBA. We're trying to figure out how coverage works, and whether it makes sense for him to be on my HDHP plan. The main benefit to him being on my plan is I get an employer contribution to the HSA for dependent and it doubles my HSA contribution limit. One downside is it's a higher premium. The other downside may be from which insurance acts as primary. There seems to be a set of rules to follow to determine primary. There's a coordination of benefits process that seems dependent on a number of things. In our case, his mom and I are not together, and he's with me for the majority of the year so I believe mine will be primary. But even under the birthday rule, mine would still be primary as my birthday is earlier in the year. The problem is if we both get a HDHP. My deductible will be higher than his mom's, and once we meet the deductible, all medical services, excluding prescriptions are covered in full (yes, you read that right. i believe this is unusual as it sounds like what would happen if we meet the maximum OOP), so I don't think her insurance will ever be active... It seems only beneficial to have her insurance if she takes a non-HDHP plan. Now if she doesn't get a non HDHP plan, then I think it would be advantageous as the the amount that I pay towards my insurance's deductible will be processed by her insurance and may result in a lower amount. Is all of this understanding correct?

You're selling investments to pay for your life, that means you have income higher than subsidy thresholds. Best way to get those subsidies again is to stop selling assets for income. There's no magic bullet here. If you live on only your wages, you can apply for the subsidies. If you live on more than your wages with investments, you lose those subsidies. If you sell your investments all at once, you'll pay a lot more in taxes than you need to and you'd still be collecting income from interest so your income would still be higher than wages. Whether that keeps you below these subsidy thresholds is matter of calculation. But if you currently have to sell assets to meet your income/expense needs, you'll need just as much interest from savings accounts to meet those needs unless you change your spending habits.
